profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This CyrusOne campus sits in Loudoun County, Virginia, in and around Sterling, part of the Northern Virginia Ashburn area data center corridor. Wikipedia coverage of CyrusOne states the company purchased 40 acres in Loudoun County in June 2016 for data center construction. CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, went public in 2013, and was taken private in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
NVA8 publishes 24 MW of IT capacity across 154,230 square feet of technical space. That works out to roughly 156 watts per square foot of IT load, a density consistent with mixed enterprise and cloud workloads rather than the highest-density AI training environments. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 24 MW of IT load is roughly 600 racks; at 10 kW per rack, a common colocation baseline, the same power supports around 2,400 racks. The operator has not published a per-rack power figure, so the actual rack count is not determinable from the spec page alone. No certifications are listed on the operator's spec page for this facility.

Within Virginia, this site ranks fourth among the five facilities on this site that carry a published megawatt figure, out of 326 mapped facilities total. Those five facilities sum to 233 MW of published IT capacity, and NVA8's 24 MW represents roughly ten percent of that figure. The remaining 321 mapped Virginia facilities publish no capacity figure here, so the 233 MW total almost certainly understates the state's real installed base by a wide margin.

Virginia, and Loudoun County specifically, is the largest data center market in the world by most measures, which means NVA8 sits inside the densest concentration of fiber, power infrastructure, and network interconnection in North America. Sterling is adjacent to the Ashburn corridor where that concentration is highest. Whether 24 MW is material to an AI buyer depends entirely on workload type: it is a meaningful footprint for inference or cloud-adjacent AI services, but it is a small footprint for large-scale distributed training, which today routinely requires campus-level power an order of magnitude larger.
